Subject: TruMed Dedicated inference — quick sizing kickoff

Alex / TruMed team —

Thanks for the productive demo last week. To get the Dedicated capacity quote and a recommended GPU SKU mix we need a few quick data points so we can map to H100 / A100 / L4 tradeoffs. If you can share answers inline that will speed things up: 

- Primary workload: generation (long instructions + 8k-32k context), embeddings, or mixture?
- Typical tokens per request (mean) and peak tokens per request (95p)?
- Requests per second (avg) and peak TPS window (1m)?
- Latency SLO for 95p of requests (ms)?
- Concurrency (number of simultaneous sessions/users during peak)?
- Do you plan to pin to specific model weights or use dynamic model routing?
- Any regulatory constraints (KMS/HSM, audit log retention)?

What we usually do: recommend H100 where memory/KV cache is binding (very long context, large model family), A100 for cost-efficient throughput at medium context lengths, and L4 for scaled embedding/low-cost burst offload where low latency per small request matters. But we want to size against your numbers and propose a reserve/burst split.

If it's easier, I attached a short worksheet you can fill (trumed_sku_workbook.xlsx). Happy to hop on a 30-min sizing call once you drop the numbers.

Thanks —
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Ben —

Thanks, great summary. Quick answers below and I pasted a couple notes from engineering.

- Primary workload: mixture. 60% long-form generation (internal clinical summarization models, average context ~16k tokens, spikes to 48k for full patient history in rare cases), 30% embedding/semantic search, 10% short chat-style assistant requests.
- Tokens per request: mean ~2,200 tokens, 95p ~22,000 tokens (those are heavy).
- RPS: avg 12 RPS, peak 95th-minute bursts up to 180 RPS (we expect spiky traffic around business hours).
- Latency SLO: generation 95p < 1.8s (for user-facing flows), embedding requests prefer <200ms.
- Concurrency: peak simultaneous generation sessions ~120.
- Model routing: we plan to use a pinned, validated model family for clinical generation for regulatory traceability; other embeddings models may be switched.
- Reg: SOC 2 + HIPAA; KMS required; audit logs mandatory.

Engineering notes: long-context runs are memory-heavy and we cannot tolerate OOMs; for the 48k spike we can accept fallback to a lower-context approximation but need predictable failover.

Alex Shepard
Head of ML Infrastructure, TruMed Analytics

Alex —

Appreciate the detail, that helps a lot. Based on your profile (heavy long-context generation with rare 48k spikes, plus strict latency SLOs for interactive flows and embedding volume), here are our recommended guardrails and a proposed Dedicated fleet mix. The high-level goal: avoid OOMs for long-context pinned model while keeping cost-efficient throughput for the rest of the workload.

High-level recommendations (short):
- Reserve a baseline pool of H100s for pinned long-context generation (model family for clinical summarization). H100 memory and NVLink/KV cache behavior gives the most predictable long-context behavior at scale.
- Use A100 (80GB) as the throughput workhorse for medium-context generation and high-concurrency generation where batch efficiency buys cost reduction.
- Offload embeddings and short assistant calls to an L4 pool (GPU-accelerated but lower-cost) and use that pool for burst/scale when possible.

Suggested fleet split (initial reserve commit):
- H100 reserved: 18% of total VMs (sized to cover concurrent 120 sessions at avg 16k, with room for prefetch/prefix caching). This covers your pinned model and leaves headroom for KV cache.
- A100 reserved: 52% of total VMs for steady generation throughput and to absorb most of the 180 RPS bursts through batching and multiplexing.
- L4 reserved: 10% reserved for embeddings and low-latency short requests; 20% burst (on-demand) to cover peak embedding volume.

Sizing rationale (concise):
- Memory/KV: For 16k–48k contexts the working set is dominated by KV cache; H100 80GB+ interconnect is the safer path for pinned models to avoid eviction or offloading.
- Latency: A100 with tuned batching achieves the 95p <1.8s for medium-length generation when we limit max sequence size per request and use adaptive batching. L4 gives sub-200ms for embeddings at scale.
- Cost: A100 yields the best tokens-per-dollar on steady-state generation, so it should be the largest portion of the commit. H100 carries premium but necessary for the critical pinned model. L4 reduces unit cost for embeddings.

Operational fallbacks and runbook notes:
- Fallback policy: if H100 pool saturates, route non-critical long-context requests to an approximated path on A100 with truncated context + pay or degraded-quality flag in response (we can return a standardized warning payload). We will instrument this as a measurable failure metric and expose it in the Console for SLA triggers.
- Cache strategy: enable prefix caching for clinical summaries; maintain per-model KV hit-rate telemetry to inform auto-scaling thresholds.
- Reserve vs burst: recommend a 70% commit / 30% burst strategy initially. That gives predictable latency and a cheaper op-ex while covering spikes with burst L4 and A100 capacity.

Next-step deliverables we will provide in 48 hours:
- A sizing workbook populated with baseline VM counts and token-cost estimates (attached: trumed_sku_workbook.xlsx).
- Reserve quote PDF (reserve_quote_v1.pdf) for procurement with 12-month and 24-month options.
- A short runbook describing the fallback behavior and telemetry keys we will surface in the Redwood Console.

Please review the split above — if you want a more conservative memory posture for the 48k extreme we can increase H100 headroom (moves cost up ~12%). If procurement prefers a lower commit, we can show a 50% commit / 50% burst scenario and the expected latency/cost tradeoffs.

I'm looping Dev to help with the detailed VM counts and to schedule a 60-minute technical sizing call if you want to walk through the sizing workbook together.
